newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION-INDIA STRATEGY-WHERE ANGELS FEAR TO TREAD-ING BARINGS.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-INDIA STRATEGY-WHERE ANGELS FEAR TO TREAD-ING BARINGS.

text.p: - In a December strategy piece titled "Where
Angels Fear to Tread," securities firm ING Barings warns investors to be cautious in first quarter 1997 allocations for the Indian market
THE PURGE IS IN FULL SWING
In the November issue of the Market Monitor we talked of the great purge of the Indian stock market. This affected all of its constituents namely investors, corporates, exchanges and intermediaries.
The purge is now in full swing but is far from complete. In the meantime, the Sensex has lost another 10 percent in November and is actually trading near its CY96 low, reached on 25 January 1996.
As 1996 is about to end, it is time to review the market's performance over the year and to evolve strategies for 1997.
$50 BLN INVESTED IN EMERGING MARKET EQUITIES IN 1996
Looking back, the chips were also down in December 1995 and the market was trading at close to its low for the year.
Domestic investors' net worth was eroding rapidly and both country funds and GDRs were close to yearly bottoms, indicating that FIIs had not gained either.

1995 had been the worst year since the decade began for emerging markets as a whole; it resulted in a measly US$15.0 billion in cross-border equity flows, compared to the record US$62.4 billion in 1993 and moderate US$39.9 billion in 1994.

However, there were great hopes of a revival in emerging markets in 1996 (after a two-year breather); these came true with an estimated US$50 billion being invested in emerging market equities in CY96, which is over three times the net flow in CY95.
..HAD A DRAMATIC IMPACT ON EMERGING MARKETS INCLUDING INDIA

The sudden surge of cross-border investment flows in 1QCY96 had a dramatic impact on several emerging markets, including India, with the Sensex zooming up by 44 percent from the January bottom by the end of 2QCY96.
In fact an estimated US$30 billion went into emerging markets in just six months compared to the US$15 billion over the previous 12 months!
India received a fair share of this investment and has been consistently achieving a 10 percent share of all investment that has flowed into emerging markets since mid-1993.

This is a fairly high weighting and is close to the expected peak performance in the next few years, as foreign ownership of Indian stocks (currently about 8 percent) draws closer to the emerging markets benchmark of 11 percent.

On a relative basis, emerging market equity flows are either stagnant or slipping slightly and 1997 is not expected to be significantly different from 1996. Therefore, the performance of the Indian stock market in 1997 will be determined by the performance of the economy and corporates rather than global liquidity flows.
..BUT ENTHUSIASM WILL PROBABLY WANE IN FIRST QUARTER 1997
We believe that in 1QCY97, FIIs will not be as enthusiastic to invest in India as they were in 1QCY96, due to dramatic changes in the underlying story.

The major factor prompting robust FII investment (10 percent of all emerging market and 20 percent of Asian equity flow) during the last three years, despite the fact that they rarely gained from investing in India, has been the continuity of economic reforms, sustained economic growth and spectacular corporate earnings growth.
During the course of the year, the foundations of the FII investment argument were rudely shaken and there does not seem to be any light at the end of the tunnel.
GENERAL ELECTION WAS CATALYST FOR INVESTOR DISENCHANTMENT

In January 1996, political uncertainty was increasing due to impending parliamentary elections. However, it was widely believed that the process of liberalisation and economic reforms initiated by P V Narasimha Rao's Congress Government would continue unabated, due to a political consensus cutting across party lines.

However, voters did not give a clear verdict in the general election, leading to a hung parliament and the formation of an unexpected coalition government of 13 disparate parties holding diverse views on the merits of economiic reform and on the process of liberalisaton itself.

We recommended a 'SELL' on the Indian market (of. Daily Preview dated 13 May 1996, Sensex - 3750.40) as we feared that the break in the reforms process and the impending economic slowdown, along with evaporating corporate earnings growth would lead to disenchantment among investors (particularly FIIs) later in the year.
Today, there is widespread disillusionment over the lack of political will to forge a consensus and unshackle the Indian economy further.

There are fears that some of the reforms (especially in the financial sector) are being rolled back. It is disturbing to note that the finance minister is coaxing the populace to spend merrily to run down inventories (Keynesian theory?) instead of saving for capital formation.
He is also coaxing banks to take more risks when lending, while the latter would prefer to stick to prudential norms in view of the industrial slowdown and probable shakeout.
..EXACERBATING DOUBTS OF AN ECONOMIC SLOWDOWN
At the beginning of the year the investment argument was that the stock market had technically bottomed and that the underlying economic fundamentals and corporate growth were sound.
However, we feared an economic slowdown and rapidly falling corporate earnings growth during 1996 and subsequent events have proved us right, thus questioning the major investment thesis of 1996.

Today, even if investors are not convinced about our argument of a recessionary trend, the impending economic crisis led by a ballooning fiscal deficit and internal debt trap and the business shakeout due to the side-effects of liberalisation, they seriously doubt the ability of the economy and corporates to reverse the downtrend quickly.
This is the most significant change in perception since FIIs decided to pump in a record US$3 billion in domestic equities and another US$1.4 billion into Indian GDRs in 1996 to date.
BOLD ECONOMIC REFORMS ARE NEEDED
We believe the economy is poised for a shakeout similar to the one witnessed in the early nineties. The balance of payments crisis has been replaced by an internal debt trap.
The gross fiscal deficit this year will be among the highest of the decade and the majority of state governments will be facing their worst financial crisis.
These serious issues need widespread and bold economic reforms over the next two years and cannot be resolved by mere tinkering with monetary policy as is widely believed.
SHRINKING CORPORATE PROFITABILITY WILL LEAD TO SURVIVAL OF
THE FITTEST
Indian corporates have displayed spectacular earnings growth in the last three years thanks to a booming capital market and spectacular consumption growth.
However, India is a fragile economy with a small consumer base thanks to the uneven distribution of income. The gradient of the income pyramid is rising, due to the lack of a percolation effect.
Hence the economy cyclically exhibits an exhaustion of demand for a couple of years following robust consumption for three-four years.
This demand fatigue coupled with a bombed-out capital market and rapidly expanding capacities in most industries will lead to shrinking corporate profitability.

The pain of liberalisation witnessed through growing competition (internal as well as external) will only accelerate the business shakeout, leading to the survival of the fittest in the next two years.
CAUTION IS ADVISED WHEN ALLOCATING FOR FIRST QUARTER 1997
We believe the market has sensed the impending danger in economic and corporate performance but has not sufficiently discounted it due to a lack of conclusive evidence.
Hence, it is still skidding and is in the process of forming a long-term bottom. We think the process will continue into the next quarter with unquantifiable damage to stock values in the process.

Therefore, it is advisable to avoid bottom-fishing and to delay further investment, at least until the grim realities in the capital market environment have been adequately factored in. One may compare the present Indian market to Thailand, which is hovering around its three-year low and expect it to perform like Brazil did early this year once the crisis is recognised as such and the political will to handle it firmly emerges.
Hence, we recommend emerging market asset allocators to critically review their past India investment theories and portfolio performance and be cautious with 1QCY97 asset allocations.
(The opinions expressed in this article reflect the views of the author only. They should not be taken as reflecting the views of Reuters)
